newsitem.title: KENYA: Finance, reforms to dominate UN environment forum.
newsitem.headline: Finance, reforms to dominate UN environment forum.

text.p: Financial woes facing the U.N. environment agency and reforms demanded by Western donors will dominate a meeting in Kenya of the agency's legislative arm, diplomats said on Sunday.

Ministers and government representatives from around 100 countries will gather in Kenya for the start on Monday of the two-week meeting of the United Nations Environment Programme's Governing Council.
The meeting, which takes place every two years, is normally used to approve a programme on managing natural resources and improving the environment.
But this year's forum will be sidetracked by talk of reforms and financial woes facing the agency due to the reluctance of Western donors to pay their dues.

"This session will be unusual because it will be revising UNEP programmes due to drastic reduction of its budget," said Shafqat Kakakhel, Pakistan Ambassador to Kenya and permanent representative to UNEP, an organisation set up in 1972.
"Financial matters and the role and future policy of UNEP will come up prominently during the session," he added.
A London-based environmental expert told Reuters by telephone from Nairobi that UNEP's entire role and structures will come under review in the meeting.
"Two issues will dominate the meeting: the work UNEP does and also the very existence of the organisation," he said.
"There is also a big divide over whether UNEP should continue to be based in Kenya," the expert added.
UNEP, the only U.N. agency based in the developing world, is reeling from financial problems.
Key Western donors such as Japan, United States of America, Britain, France and Italy are reluctant to pay, arguing UNEP has become less effective since the 1992 Earth Summit.
As a result UNEP has seen its budget drop sharply over the last few years as donors link further funding to reforms in the agency.
From a budget of $160 million during UNEP's 1991-92 programme, budget provision fell to $105 million in the last two years and even then only $62.5 million was disbursed by donors.
UNEP is preparing a budget of up to $80 million for the next two years but many experts doubt the powerful West will pay.

"There are a lot of fears, genuine fears that even $80 million planned for in the budget will not be achieved at all. The Western world seems keen to starve the agency into reform," an African ambassador told Reuters.
The United States has spearheaded calls for a cut in UNEP's budget as part of its attacks on U.N. agencies it considers inefficient or outdated.
New U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan has promised to reform UNEP and has made U.N. reform a constant theme since his election last December.
Washington vetoed his predecessor, Boutros Boutros-Ghali, charging him with failure to press reform of the 185-nation organisation with sufficient vigour.
Critics charge UNEP with lack of focus and say the organisation suffers from staff demoralisation, isolation from other U.N. agencies and low quality of staff it can recruit to its Nairobi base.
